power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Introduction: Prehabilitation aims to optimise psychological status, but psychological provision largely addresses existing distress and what preparation for treatment consists of is unclear as prehabilitation services scale up.
We asked how patients experience it, what enables or undermines it, and how their circumstances shape what they can use.
We searched CINAHL, MEDLINE and PsycINFO from inception, last searched 22 May 2026, for peer-reviewed English-language qualitative studies of adults' experiences of multimodal cancer prehabilitation.

Eligible programmes combined at least two of exercise, nutrition and psychological support, and either targeted psychological outcomes or included an element with a stated psychological function; measurement alone did not qualify.
Two reviewers appraised reports using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme checklist plus four domains covering staff training, fidelity, adherence and participants' words.
We synthesised findings by meta-ethnography.
No external funding.
Registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023434123).
Results: Seventeen reports (2021-2026), predominantly surgical and from six high-income countries, drew on 14 independent samples and 230 patients.

Across three constructs and 12 subthemes, patients experienced psychological preparation as having something to act on, discovering what their bodies could do, understanding and managing what was coming, being taken seriously and kept going, and not being alone.
These functions arose through exercise, dietary support and relationships with staff and peers, not only explicitly psychological input.
Prehabilitation added to preparations already under way.
Relevance, timing, burden and continuity after surgery enabled or undermined preparation, depending on patients' beliefs, capacity, demands and support networks.
Discussion: Evidence came almost entirely from engagers, and staff training, adherence and fidelity were sparsely reported.
Psychological preparation did not map onto a discrete component; it arose where what a programme offered matched what a patient could use.
Services should build psychological function into how prehabilitation is delivered, who delivers it, and how it is matched to patients.

Prehabilitation is proactive preparation, before and during cancer treatment, intended to build the physical, nutritional and psychological reserve patients need to withstand and recover from treatment [1, 2].

text.text: It involves screening and needs-based assessment, enabling individualised, often multimodal prescription of exercise, nutrition and psychological support [1, 2].
text.formatted: It involves screening and needs-based assessment, enabling individualised, often multimodal prescription of exercise, nutrition and psychological support <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: Psychological status is therefore part of what prehabilitation is for, not an optional extra, and prehabilitation differs from general psychosocial care in being organised around an impending treatment.
Anxiety, depression, self-harm and suicide are more common after a cancer diagnosis, particularly in the first year [3], and in more deprived groups [4].
text.formatted: Anxiety, depression, self-harm and suicide are more common after a cancer diagnosis, particularly in the first year <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>, and in more deprived groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Depression after diagnosis is also associated with poorer survival [5].
text.formatted: Depression after diagnosis is also associated with poorer survival <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Psychological input is also less readily taken up once distress has appeared and treatment has begun [6].
text.formatted: Psychological input is also less readily taken up once distress has appeared and treatment has begun <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Psychological prehabilitation therefore has two aims: to treat existing difficulties, and to reduce future ones [1].
text.formatted: Psychological prehabilitation therefore has two aims: to treat existing difficulties, and to reduce future ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: The revised UK guidelines accordingly ask services to assess symptoms alongside illness perceptions, coping and self-efficacy, which predict later distress [1, 7].
text.formatted: The revised UK guidelines accordingly ask services to assess symptoms alongside illness perceptions, coping and self-efficacy, which predict later distress <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref>.

text.text: But what optimised psychological status amounts to is not specified.
Exercise and nutrition have proximal targets linked to recovery -fitness, strength, nutritional markers [2].
text.formatted: Exercise and nutrition have proximal targets linked to recovery -fitness, strength, nutritional markers <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Of 140 prehabilitation studies, 89% gave a fitness rationale and 33% a psychological one [8].
text.formatted: Of 140 prehabilitation studies, 89% gave a fitness rationale and 33% a psychological one <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Where it is assessed, psychological status is defined reactively, around difficulties already present [1, 9] rather than around readiness for future treatment, which patients described as a "mindset to have surgery": confidence in what to expect and in coping, motivation, and anxiety that is expected but manageable [10].

text.text: Programmes containing a psychological component do reduce overall postoperative complications (RR 0.73, 95%CI 0.60-0.89) [11], without showing what that component contributed.

text.text: This gap is about to scale up, as prehabilitation moves from trials into policy and services in England.

The National Cancer Plan for England commits to a national, digital-first prehabilitation offer from 2028 and to a personalised assessment of every patient's physical, mental health and social needs [12], taking forward the Ten-Year Health Plan's shifts from sickness to prevention, hospital to community, and analogue to digital [13].

text.text: Services elsewhere are on the same trajectory [14].
text.formatted: Services elsewhere are on the same trajectory <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: A programme nevertheless delivers only what patients can use. [1], and what is delivered is often poorly reported [9]; so trials tell us little about what preparation consists of for patients or what within a programme produces it.

text.text: Two qualitative syntheses have asked what determines participation in prehabilitation before major surgery [15] and adherence to it [16], coding patient accounts into existing behavioural frameworks.

text.text: Neither examined psychological preparation as an outcome or looked for it outside components labelled psychological.

To address these gaps, we synthesised qualitative studies of patients' experiences of multimodal prehabilitation with a psychological function, appraising how far each report described the programme it studied.

We asked how people with cancer experience psychological preparation, which components, relationships and delivery processes enabled or undermined it, and how patients' circumstances, capacity and the timing of the offer shaped what they could use.
We follow PRISMA reporting [17], registered the review with PROSPERO (CRD42023434123; which is the protocol), and took a critical realist approach.
text.formatted: We follow PRISMA reporting <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>, registered the review with PROSPERO (CRD42023434123; which is the protocol), and took a critical realist approach.

text.text: Searches to January 2024 informed an earlier version (Hussain et al., preprint, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/8pvfu_v1).

text.text: After the provisional 2024 synthesis, we respecified the question around psychological preparation and dropped the requirement to distinguish experiences of psychological components (preparation extended beyond them).

Eligibility followed the PI(C)OS framework:  Population: adults (18+) with a cancer diagnosis;  Intervention: programmes comprising at least two of the three core guideline domains-exercise, nutrition and psychological support [1]-and either aiming to address psychological outcomes or including an element with a stated psychological or psychosocial function; psychological outcome measurement alone did not qualify.

text.text: We focused on multimodal programmes to inform the combined model of care recommended in UK guidance [1], examining patients' experiences of psychological preparation when different intervention domains are offered together.

text.text: We defined domains by content rather than how it was delivered, so a single resource addressing more than one domain qualified.
Eligibility concerned the programme offered, not the number of domains each participant received.

Programmes extending into rehabilitation were eligible if they included an identifiable prehabilitation phase; where phases could not be separated, we retained the report and treated attribution to prehabilitation as uncertain;  Outcomes: participants' experiences of prehabilitation; and,  Study type: qualitative studies using a formal method of analysis, from which data on the programme could be extracted.

On 13 January 2024 and 22 May 2026, we searched CINAHL, Medline, and PsycINFO from inception for peer-reviewed, English-language studies, using PI(C)OS terms combined with Boolean logic and a subject librarian's support (Supporting Information Table S1 gives the scripts).

text.text: We hand-searched relevant reviews and included reports.
At each stage one reviewer screened all titles and abstracts (AH in 2024, ZU in 2026) and a second screened them independently (MB).
Discrepancies were resolved by consensus, refining the criteria.
One was adjudicated by MR.
AH (2024) and ZU (2026) extracted data using an a priori form, cross-checked by MB (Tables 2 and 3).

text.text: For the update, we also recorded the provider, label, and level (universal, targeted or specialist) of psychological or psychosocial elements.

We retained extracts describing a psychological or psychosocial experience, need or impact, for example, emotion, appraisals of control, agency or self-efficacy, coping, motivation, identity, and relational support.
We included physical, practical, and nutritional material only when its psychological function or bearing on engagement was explicit.
In mixed samples, accounts from others (professionals, partners) provided context but not first-or second-order data unless patient contributions were independently identifiable.

We used the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) qualitative checklist [18, 19], which applies across diverse qualitative designs and theoretical positions, to characterise, rather than score or exclude, studies.

text.text: Because the revised question re-specified our phenomenon of interest, we treated the 2024 synthesis as provisional.

We extracted the seven additional reports in full, re-read the earlier extracts and constructs against source findings, added constructs not captured earlier, and re-translated all 17 reports together.

We coded each new extract as confirming, extending, contradicting or adding to the earlier interpretation, mapped the earlier subthemes onto the revised framework, and carried forward nothing without a psychological or psychosocial function.
As a sensitivity check, we examined whether each subtheme remained after excluding reports with uncertain CASP judgements.

text.text: They were published in 2021-2026 and drew on 14 independent samples and 230 patients: A and C report subsets of B's interview sample, and H a subset of I's.
Samples of 5-45 patients came from the UK (eight reports), Denmark (four), Canada (two), and the USA, the Netherlands and Australia (one each), with mean or median ages of 54-69.
All but two reports used interviews (J: questionnaire; L: focus group with observation); A-C also collected written records.
Only I deliberately included non-engagers (2/18); M sampled all referrals but did not report engagement, and in O we included only participants who had experienced prehabilitation.
In D and L, prehabilitation-specific findings could be distinguished only in part.
All reports met CASP criteria for aims, methodology, design and findings (Table 4).

text.text: Main limitations were in recruitment, reflexivity, and transparency of their analysis: five underreported recruitment, seven researcher-participant relationships and two theme development.
Data ranged from 5-10-minute interviews by service staff or one 23-minute focus group to in-depth interviews.
Intervention reporting was weaker: four reports reported staff training or supervision, five monitored adherence and one assessed fidelity.
The latter noted its fidelity procedures had little impact and delivery varied with facilitators' experience and confidence.
Delivery as intended and exposure to each component were therefore mostly unclear.

We developed three third-order constructs: (1) what patients experienced as psychological preparation; (2) what enabled or undermined this preparation; and (3) how patients' existing beliefs, circumstances and relationships shaped both.
Twelve subthemes sat within them.
Table 5 shows the reports contributing to each subtheme.

text.text: TABLE 5 ABOUT HERE T1 What patients experienced as psychological preparation Patients described functions rather than programme components.
These arose through exercise, dietary support, contact with staff and other patients, as well as through explicitly psychological input (E) (Q01).
Prehabilitation gave patients something to act on in a period they could not otherwise influence.
Where everything seemed "unmanageable and hopeless", it let them focus on the important things and do something before surgery that might pay off afterwards (N) (Q07).
What they acted on was small and concrete.

Patients put a cross on a leaflet every day, wrote down what they had managed on a day when not much else happened (A, B) (Q03, Q02), kept a food journal with the dietitian (O) (Q08), or took direction about exercise, nutrition and coping (K) (Q06).
Enrolment, appointments and regular contact gave "rhythm" (P).
It also took focus away from cancer (H), and completing meaningful tasks gave a sense of control (C).
What patients found controllable was their own body and conduct, not the disease: "something you can control yourself, because you can't control the cancer" (E, P) (Q04, Q05).
Patients also found out what they and their bodies could do, and their confidence was based on their lived experience.
Repeated assessment made capability visible, including to patients who had thought themselves fit enough already (M).
So did being able to "clearly feel the improvement" and find themselves "the first one up the hills" within weeks (N) (Q13).
Others felt better able to "fight" (K) (Q12), or came to value a strong body despite feeling "really bad" on chemotherapy (O) (Q14).
Reports named this effect differently: selfefficacy (E), or confidence and self-esteem (H, D) (Q09, Q10).

Only one report, with the most transparent sampling and the fullest account of its own conduct, highlighted the adverse side to this effect: where patients could feel no change, confidence fell and habits formed during the programme lapsed within days (P) (Q11, Q15).
The other form was acting on feelings directly.
Grounding and breathing filled the "void" between the facts on paper and living through them (Q) (Q17, Q18).
Patients still used stress-management recordings during adjuvant chemotherapy (K) (Q20), and exercise itself became a moment to relax before a "nerve-wracking procedure" (P) (Q24).
Some of this outlasted the programme: patients could tell themselves they were "as prepared as you can be" (N) (Q19).
But it was not always usable: one patient found the counsellor helpful, needed more, and "gritted my teeth and got on with it" instead (M) (Q22).
Patients experienced relationships with staff as psychologically active, and professional involvement supported their motivation and adherence (A, B, C, E, F, H, I, J).
What made it work was being treated as a person with a view.
Patients described a nurse who "took everything I said seriously" (D) (Q27), staff "like having a friend there all the way through" (M) (Q28), and a service where "no one feels judged" (L) (Q32).
Being known in this way made it safe to ask, to disclose and to keep taking part.
Expertise removed specific fears.
Patients would not trust an ordinary trainer with "this particular situation" (K) (Q31) and wanted someone "educated in that field" who saw them "as a human being" (Q) (Q29).
A surgeon's confirmation that a four-week wait carried no risk was itself a relief (N).
Relationships also sustained effort, and whether that helped depended on how it was negotiated.
Regular appointments and a little push to go the extra mile supplied accountability when motivation dipped (K, P) (Q33).
One woman said "there had to be real pressure" and that staff had to "keep an eye on me" (B) (Q25); another that patients do not want to be "pigeonholed" (C) (Q26).
The relationship took time to build: where staffing was short, staff "answer questions and that's probably it" (O) (Q30).
Programmes brought patients together to deliver exercise, and patients found a social effect that was rarely designed for.
Being among others in the same position gave validation, knowledge, and a change of perspective (B, E, G, H, Q).
Patients drew "mental strength" from watching post-operative patients back in the class and doing well (G) (Q34), and encouraged each other "without realizing it" (P) (Q38).
Classes were where surgery and difficult feelings could be discussed (D).
Meeting someone who had already had a difficult operation provided reassurance (F), and where patients attended hospital alone the programme helped them feel supported (K) (Q35).
What patients accepted depended on what the group was for and on who was in it.
A group "working to the same goal" of getting fit was welcome, but the same patient would not have joined one where she had to "compare cancers, or stages" (O) (Q37).
In a group of "elderly men mainly", a woman with ovarian cancer found that "you are very lonely when you are not in the common denominator group" (M) (Q36).
Within a single study patients disagreed, some expecting peer contact before transplant to help and others to worsen distress (Q).
Group contact prepared patients where they could recognise themselves in the others.
What enabled preparation and what undermined it were often the same featuresrelevance, timing, burden, continuity -working in opposite directions for different patients.
Patients wanted a programme that recognised their situation and fitted their circumstances (A, B, E, F, G, I).
They wanted material to be relevant to "my situation" rather than general (B) (Q40), and classes had to feel like "personal classes just for you" even in a group (G) (Q41).
Patients resented what had been organised without considering what they wanted (I) (Q42) and mismatches limited engagement with the whole programme (C, D).
Psychological support was most acceptable where it was available and "not labelled" as such (H) (Q39).
Relevance could fail at several levels.
Patients were given information without being told what prehabilitation was for (M, O) (Q45).
What they wanted differed between the exercise, dietary and psychological parts (K), and some equated prehabilitation with exercise, knowing little of its other elements (N).

How much information was right differed between patients even in the same report: some were "deluged with information" at diagnosis, others found it enough because "you can choose yourself" (M) (Q43, Q44).
Format divided them the same way: remote delivery widening access for some and removing personal contact for others (O).
Psychological input too had to match the amount patients wanted (Q).
Where it did not, it did not register as support: a drop-in chat was not what one patient needed (O) (Q46), and a request for psychological help before surgery was never acted on (O) (Q47).
Patients often wanted prehabilitation introduced early, but not all at once.

Reports agreed that early introduction was valuable (C, E, F, I) (Q48, Q49), ideally around diagnosis as a "crucial time" (Q) (Q55), but briefly rather than in detail that "can end up putting people off" (Q50).
It allowed patients to prepare at their own pace during a four-week wait (N) and one patient thought it "better to know everything than only bits and pieces" (O) (Q54).
Against early introduction, being overwhelmed was the most common reason for not taking part at all, with information arriving while patients were "still digesting the diagnosis" (K) (Q53).

Interviewees in one report were told everything at once when they were "too ill to deal with it" (M) (Q51), and an early offer close to surgery led patients to think the classes would be of little use (D).
What seemed to separate these positions was not when the offer arrived but whether it matched what the patient could use.
A psychosexual consultation held before surgery was about "what might happen" rather than "my own situation" (N) (Q52).
Where prehabilitation took place mattered largely because of what it cost patients to attend (A, B, C, D, E, J) (Q56, Q57, Q58).
Treatment side effects were the most common barrier: fatigue and post-surgical tiredness meant patients "would just sleep all day long" (K) (Q61) or could not re-engage (P).
The programme's own demands could exhaust patients, one coming out "completely exhausted" and learning to "set your own boundaries" (P) (Q60).
What reduced the cost was largely administrative.

Appointments were scheduled alongside existing hospital visits, with travel reimbursement and parking vouchers (K), moved online where patients could not attend (M, O) (Q62), or someone worked "in the background to organise all the visits" (Q) (Q63).
But capacity could be depleted before the offer was made, with one patient already "mentally exhausted" and wanting to be left alone (I) (Q59).
Support that ended at surgery was experienced as loss rather than completion.
Patients contrasted "fantastic treatment in hospital" with being "kind of on your own" afterwards, sometimes feeling abandoned or feeling responsible for re-establishing contact (D) (Q64, Q65).
Other endings were as abrupt: being held "by the collar over a cliff" (P) (Q67), or simply "goodbye" after recovery (M) (Q68).
Where support continued, patients valued it.

Access to the prehabilitation team on discharge reinforced the changes they had made (E) (Q66), and one patient still in psychotherapy found it brought "pre-surgery" and "after surgery" into context, working better for her afterwards than it would have before (O) (Q69).
Some resumed the prehabilitation routine by themselves (K), while post-operative advice to rest sometimes undid what the programme had started (P).
T3 Patients' identities, circumstances and relationships What patients brought with them shaped both themes above.

Their beliefs about themselves, the demands already on them, and the people around them determined what counted as preparation and how it worked out. 3a The person who arrives: identity, beliefs and valued futures Patients did not arrive as blank slates, and what they already believed about themselves governed whether prehabilitation seemed necessary.
Expecting "physio care afterwards" to suffice (I) (Q71), feeling already fit enough, and judging psychological support unnecessary reduced perceived need ( C, D, H).

text.text: Wanting to help future patients by taking part in the research (B), a positive mindset (E), or a pragmatic "get this thing out of me" (F) (Q70) worked the other way.
Being "very independent and resilient" meant not seeing a need, though not that others would not benefit (M) (Q73).
For one patient preparing at all would have meant admitting she "might not survive", so she prepared nothing (C) (Q72).
Beliefs about psychology shaped uptake of it as a distinct component.
A referral could be read as the care team's judgement that the patient was not coping (Q).

Seeing oneself as a strong person could work either way: protective for some, and for others a route to avoidance and later overwhelm, one patient who thought herself "relatively a strong person" unable to recognise her own anxiety (Q) (Q74).
Patients also differed in the kind of future they valued.
Most spoke of returning to normality, but one rejected this because "normality for me is not going to be enough" (O) (Q75).
For others, anticipated incontinence and loss of sexual function mattered more than cure: one would rather risk not being cured than lose "a proper life" (N) (Q76).
Once surgery was decided, those patients engaged eagerly in preparation.
Others approached the future more provisionally -"we'll see how it goes" -which shaped how far motivation and support became action (P) (Q77).
Patients prepared in ways the programmes did not propose: housekeeping, packing hospital bags, work plans, wills, insurance papers and funeral arrangements.
Preparing in these ways gave patients security and control in a situation without them otherwise (A, B, C -linked reports from one research group) (Q78, Q80).
An independent fourth report confirms it: one patient got her will straight because it "hangs over you" and surgery "spurred me on" (O) (Q82).
Time and competing priorities constrained what was possible, so programmes had to fit flexibly around the work, commitments and appointments patients already had (A, B, C, D, E, J) (Q79).
Life stage, dependants and work determined how much patients could absorb, younger ones struggling "to work and raise kids and deal with this at the same time" (Q) (Q83).
And though prehabilitation was free where it was studied, continuing the activities afterwards was "way too expensive" (P) (Q81).
Family and friends worked both as scaffold to the programme and as substitute for it.
Including family members was considered in A, B, C, E and J. As scaffold, family members supported engagement and adherence (A, B, E, J) (Q84) and supplied accountability and structure.

One patient exercised "every day because my family made me" (K) (Q87), another made a schedule with his wife (N) (Q89), and a husband joined the dietetic consultation so that he knew what was being asked of her (O).
A partner could be the second set of ears where "there's a lot you don't take in" (Q) (Q91) and support from others sustained motivation, one patient calling it "indispensable" (P) (Q86).
As substitute, family and friend support reduced the perceived need for professional help.
One patient with a strong network "didn't really approach any professionals" (M) (Q88), and another declined the offer because she had "the most supportive family that listen completely" (O) (Q92).
Those without a network described isolation itself as their motivation to take part (M).
Support went in the opposite direction too.
Where a partner was more affected by the diagnosis than the patient herself, she "stopped fighting him for help" (O) (Q90).
One patient had not talked about her diagnosis with her husband or children, and would rather not "bother" the friends she could have turned to (C) (Q85).
Patients prepared in their own ways as well as the programme's.
They organised their households and work, packed for hospital, made wills and drew on the people around them, which gave them security and control.
Prehabilitation added to this.

It gave patients something concrete to do, evidence of what their bodies could manage, ways to understand and handle what was coming, and relationships with staff and peers that made it easier and less lonely to keep going.
No component carried its psychological function on its own.
This function arose between what a programme offered and what a patient could recognise and use as preparation.
Patients saw little need if they thought themselves fit, expected physiotherapy afterwards to be enough, already had people who listened, or found preparing itself too threatening.
Where the offer did fit, preparation depended on what patients could use at that moment, demands within their capacity, and professionals who respected their judgement rather than overriding it.
Professional attention could feel like supportive accountability or pressure.
Early introduction could orient patients or overwhelm them.
The same element did different psychological work for different patients and at different times.
Psychological preparation was not something completed before surgery, nor a separate component alongside exercise and nutrition.
It could continue through treatment and recovery, and it depended across the pathway on what patients could use.
Where support continued after surgery, some patients carried the changes and routines they had built into recovery.
Abrupt endings left others feeling abandoned, or stopped the momentum they had built.
The reports could not isolate what any single component did.
What they showed is how patients experienced psychological preparation across a whole programme and against everything else in their lives.

In patients' experience, psychological preparation involved agency, confidence in capability, orientation to what was coming and help managing how it felt, relationships in which they felt known, and belonging among other patients.

It extended beyond reducing distress to preparedness for treatment and recovery, developing accounts of psychological readiness as a "mindset to have surgery": knowing what to expect, confidence in coping, motivation, and anxiety that remains manageable [10].

text.text: Two things follow.
Psychological function arose through exercise, dietary contact, staff relationships and peer contact, as well as explicitly psychological input.
And it materialised where what a programme offered met what a patient could recognise and use, which is why the same element prepared one patient and burdened another.
What patients could recognise depended on what they already believed about prehabilitation and about psychological support.
Our synthesis examined what taking part in cancer prehabilitation does for psychological preparation, extending what we know from earlier syntheses on who participates and who continues [15,16].
Relationships with staff did psychological work, yet few reports described how staff were prepared for it.

In one programme, co-ordinators delivering universal emotional and nutritional support had been trained for the role, yet described lacking experience with patients at diagnosis, and gave less attention to both elements because they saw them as outside their expertise (F).

Nurses delivering prehabilitation report limited training, absent specialist roles and staffing shortages [42], and psychological input delivered through existing roles can be effective where staff are trained and supervised [43].

text.text: Contact with other patients prepared people where they could recognise themselves in the group, and mismatched groups deepened isolation.
This may reflect a social identity process shown to influence health outcomes [44].

text.text: Most of these effects arose outside elements designated as psychological and varied with staffing, matching, and timing.
Services should therefore support these psychological functions deliberately through routine programme design and delivery rather than leave them to chance.

Within the guidelines' stratified model [1], universal provision would mean psychologically informed delivery across programme components; targeted provision, firstline input for identified needs from staff trained and supervised to provide it through their existing roles (e.g., exercise); and specialist provision, assessment and intervention by psychological professionals for more complex needs.

text.text: A whole-programme approach complements rather than replaces discrete psychological care.
Where services extend across surgery, continuity should also be supported.
Group composition needs attention too.
Programmes already utilise groups, so creating a common purpose, connecting patients' resources for mutual benefit, and choice about taking part could turn an incidental effect into a planned one.
What patients could use was constrained by travel, cost, treatment effects, work, and caring responsibilities.
Remote provision reduced attendance burdens for some but removed valued contact for others.
Services can address or exacerbate these inequalities [45], and criteria for equitable provision exist [46].

text.text: That is how the field will identify prehabilitation's psychological mechanisms and optimise them as deliberately as it optimises physical and nutritional status.
Almost all the evidence came from patients willing to take part who received at least some of a programme, and few studies examined how education, employment or deprivation shaped engagement.
Only one report explicitly identified programme non-engagers within its interview sample (I; n=2).
All studies were conducted in high-income countries, often within established or research-supported services, which limits transferability to other health systems.
Reporting on staff training, fidelity, and adherence was sparse, so we cannot say whether programmes were delivered as intended or how much each patient received.
Most accounts were retrospective and gathered within the delivering services, so may be positively biased.
Two reports contributed thin data for our research question and five drew on two samples, so the independent evidence is narrower than seventeen reports suggests.
Our interpretations also rest on the quotations and analyses the original authors chose to publish.
Support was thinnest for continuity after surgery and family involvement.
We included only peer-reviewed reports in English and excluded programmes with neither a stated psychological aim nor an element with a stated psychological function.
Psychological preparation did not map onto a discrete component.
It arose where what a programme offered matched what a patient could use.

Services should therefore build psychological function into how prehabilitation is delivered, who delivers it, and how it is matched to patients, and optimise it as deliberately as they optimise physical and nutritional status.
Phases of Meta-ethnography
Read studies and familiarise self with the concepts.
Extract study characteristics.
Extract raw data for the synthesis; first and second order constructs.
Determining how the studies are related Consider relationships between the identified concepts across the studies.
Translating the studies into one another Compare each concept from each paper with all the other papers to identify presence and absence, similarities and differences.
This allows for organisation into third order constructs.
Synthesising the Translations Viewing the studies as a 'whole', develop new interpretations or conceptualisations about the phenomena investigated within the study.
Decide whether the studies share similar accounts (reciprocal) or contradicting accounts (refutational).
Interpret the relationship between the third order constructs identified.
Follow the PRISMA guidance for reporting.

text.text: Making sense and managing feeling: orientation and emotional processingEmotional preparation took two forms.
One was orientation: making sense of what was happening and what could be done about it.
Staff explained that exercise would help patients "overcome this" after chemotherapy (L) (Q21), and a dietitian helped address a fear about eating that the medical team had not raised (K).
Where understanding shifted, feeling followed.
Counselling produced a more positive mental attitude alongside physical preparation (E) (Q16), and psychotherapy "rounded it all up" (O) (Q23).
